concepts.title: Vertical vs. Horizontal Scaling
concepts.description: Every capacity problem starts with the same fork in the road: make one machine bigger, or use more machines. The choice sets the ceiling, the cost curve, and the failure model of everything you build on top of it.
learningObjectives: Define vertical scaling and horizontal scaling in terms of exactly what resource is being added.
Explain the physical and economic ceiling that limits vertical scaling, including non-linear cost growth for larger instances.
Explain why horizontal scaling requires additional coordination infrastructure that vertical scaling does not.
Explain why a single machine -- no matter how large -- cannot satisfy a high-availability requirement on its own.
Given a workload description, recommend vertical or horizontal scaling and justify the choice with a concrete tradeoff.

sections.heading: Two Different Answers to "We Need More Capacity"
sections.body:
**Vertical scaling** ("scaling up") means adding more resources (CPU, RAM, faster disks, more network bandwidth) to a single existing machine. If your database runs on a `db.r5.xlarge` instance and you resize it to a `db.r5.8xlarge`, you still have one database instance, only a more powerful one. **Horizontal scaling** ("scaling out") means adding more machines that each handle a share of the total work: going from 2 application servers to 20 behind a load balancer, or adding read replicas to a database so multiple machines can serve read traffic in parallel.

A quick test tells them apart: after you scale, do you have the same number of machines running the workload (vertical), or more of them (horizontal)? The first changes how fast one machine is. The second changes how many machines can fail independently, and that difference drives cost, complexity, and what users see when something breaks.

sections.heading: The Ceiling on Vertical Scaling: Physics and Price
sections.body:
Vertical scaling hits two ceilings, at different points. The first is **physical**: at any given moment there is a largest machine you can rent or buy. In 2026 that is very large (AWS sells instances with 1,920 vCPUs and 32 TiB of RAM), but past it there is no bigger box to move to.

The second ceiling is **economic**, and it usually bites first. Inside one mainstream cloud family the price is close to linear: a `db.r5.8xlarge` costs about 4x a `db.r5.2xlarge`. The curve bends when you run out of that family. The next step up is a specialized high-memory family, a multi-socket server, or a database license priced per core, and there the cost per unit of capacity climbs, because few are sold and buyers at that size have few alternatives. Cost also becomes lumpy: one enormous machine can't be shrunk at night the way a pool of small ones can.

The third limit has nothing to do with size or price. However large it is, it is still **one machine**: one power supply, one kernel, one physical host that can fail, need a reboot for patching, or share hardware with a noisy neighbor. A very fast single point of failure is still a single point of failure.

sections.heading: What Horizontal Scaling Costs: Coordination
sections.body:
Horizontal scaling avoids both ceilings: you can keep adding commodity machines, which are cheaper per unit of capacity than the most exotic ones. In exchange you trade a hardware problem for a software and coordination problem.

Once you have more than one machine serving the same workload, you need a way to route requests across them (a load balancer, the subject of the next lesson), and you need the system's behavior to not depend on *which* machine happened to handle a given request (statelessness, also covered next). If the workload is stateful, such as a database, a cache, or a queue, you also need a way to keep multiple machines' copies of the data consistent with each other, which is where replication, sharding, and consistency tradeoffs (the CAP theorem, and the second module of this subject) come from.

None of that complexity exists with a single vertically-scaled machine, because there's only one copy of everything and nothing to keep in sync. That is why "just scale vertically" is often the right answer for as long as it holds: it postpones replication lag, failover, and cross-node consistency until you need to pay for them. Day-to-day operations change too: every deploy, config change, and secret now has to reach all the machines consistently, and a bad release can sit on some of them and not others.

sections.heading: Choosing Between Them: Sequencing, Not Ideology
sections.body:
Most systems do both, in sequence. Scale vertically first, because it needs no application changes (resize the instance, usually with a restart) and modern hardware is enormous; plenty of workloads never reach either ceiling.

Move to horizontal scaling when one of two things becomes true: you hit the vertical ceiling (there's no bigger box, or the cost curve has become absurd), or you have an availability requirement that no single machine can satisfy. The second case is the one people miss. A 99.99% target allows about 53 minutes of downtime a year, and one machine spends that on a few patch reboots and a single hardware fault; AWS's own SLA for an individual EC2 instance is only 99.5%. To promise 99.99% you need at least two independently failing machines serving traffic. Before choosing, work out which force you're facing, a capacity ceiling or a fault-domain requirement, because a bigger box only helps with the first.

examples.title: Resizing vs. Replicating a Database
examples.code:
BEFORE:
  1x db.r5.2xlarge  (8 vCPU, 64 GB RAM)   -- handling 5,000 reads/sec, CPU-bound at 85%

OPTION A (vertical):
  1x db.r5.8xlarge  (32 vCPU, 256 GB RAM) -- same single instance, 4x the resources
  -> capacity roughly 4x; at this size, roughly 4x the price too
  -> still ONE instance: one failure domain, one maintenance window, one upper bound

OPTION B (horizontal):
  1x db.r5.2xlarge (primary, handles writes)
  + 4x db.r5.2xlarge (read replicas, handle reads)
  -> read capacity ~4x (up to 5x if the primary also serves reads)
  -> 5 instances in total, so roughly 5x the original price (25% more than Option A)
  -> if any one replica dies, the other 3 keep serving reads
  -> but: replicas lag behind the primary, so reads can be slightly stale
examples.explanation: Both options buy about four times the read capacity, and Option A is a little cheaper, so price doesn't decide this one. Failure behavior and read scaling do. Option A still has one thing that can go down and take the database with it. Option B spreads reads over four replicas that fail independently, at the cost of replication lag: a client could read slightly stale data, a preview of the consistency tradeoffs later in this subject. Option B also leaves a gap: writes still depend on the one primary, so you need a failover process that promotes a replica before you can claim there is no single point of failure. The comparison also undercuts the idea that vertical is always worse value: at this size it isn't. What horizontal adds is the absence of a single point of failure for reads.

examples.title: Why the Cost Curve Bends Against You at the Top
examples.code:
Illustrative numbers: the shape is the point, no vendor's price list is quoted.

Server class         vCPU   RAM      Relative price   Price per vCPU
small (baseline)       4     16 GB     1.0x             1.00x
medium                 8     32 GB     2.1x             1.05x
large                 16     64 GB     4.6x             1.15x
2x-large              32    128 GB    10.8x             1.35x
4x-large (top tier)   64    256 GB    28.0x             1.75x
examples.explanation: Each step doubles the resources, but the price more than doubles, so price per vCPU climbs: at the top you pay 75% more per unit of compute than at the baseline. Don't expect this inside one cloud family, where doubling the size usually doubles the price. You meet it when the next size up means leaving that family for high-memory hardware, or when per-core database licenses sit on top. Before you plan a resize, look up the price per vCPU and per GB at your current size and two steps above it; that tells you whether the economic ceiling is near. The premium exists because few customers buy the very top tier, so there is less competition and the hardware is scarcer. So "vertical scaling hits a ceiling" means two things: there is no bigger box, and the biggest ones get disproportionately expensive well before you can no longer buy them.

examples.title: One Big Box vs. a Pool of Small Ones, Under Failure
examples.code:
Scenario: a traffic spike causes one machine to become unhealthy and get taken out of rotation.

ARCHITECTURE A -- one vertically-scaled machine:
  [ single large server ] -- unhealthy -- 100% of traffic has nowhere to go -- full outage

ARCHITECTURE B -- eight horizontally-scaled machines behind a load balancer:
  [LB] -> server 1 (unhealthy, removed from rotation)
       -> server 2 .. server 8 (healthy, absorb the extra load)
  -- 12.5% of capacity lost; each of the remaining 7 machines takes ~14% more load (8/7)
examples.explanation: In Architecture A, "unhealthy" and "total outage" are the same event, because there is nothing to fail over to. In Architecture B, losing one of eight machines cuts capacity by one-eighth and the system stays up, provided two things hold: the load balancer detects the unhealthy instance and stops routing to it (health checks, covered in the next lesson), and the other seven have headroom. If they were already running at 90% CPU, a 14% increase pushes them over 100% and they fail one after another. Size the pool so it survives losing a machine at peak. Containing a failure this way is often worth more than the extra capacity.

misconceptions.description: Horizontal scaling is the modern, correct approach and vertical scaling is a legacy technique you should avoid.
misconceptions.clarification: Vertical scaling is frequently the right and simplest answer: it requires no code changes and no distributed-systems complexity, and modern single machines are large enough for most workloads. Horizontal scaling trades a hardware limitation for a harder problem: coordinating multiple independently-failing machines, keeping their state consistent, and load-balancing traffic between them. Reaching for horizontal scaling before you need it (premature scaling) adds operational and cognitive cost for a problem you don't have yet. The usual sequence is vertical first, then horizontal when vertical demonstrably can't meet a capacity or availability requirement.
misconceptions.fact: Vertical scaling is frequently the right and simplest answer: it requires no code changes and no distributed-systems complexity, and modern single machines are large enough for most workloads.

misconceptions.description: If I have N servers instead of 1, my capacity is N times higher, full stop.
misconceptions.clarification: That's only true if the workload is embarrassingly parallel, meaning each unit of work is independent and never touches shared state. The moment multiple servers need to read or write the same database, cache, or lock, some of the added capacity gets consumed by contention and coordination overhead (extra network hops, lock waits, cache invalidation traffic) instead of useful work. This is the systems version of Amdahl's law. In the extreme, adding more servers past the point where a shared bottleneck (like a single non-replicated database) is already saturated buys no additional throughput at all, no matter how many app servers sit in front of it.

exercises.prompt: A checkout service runs on one machine and is CPU-bound at 500 req/s. The on-call engineer resizes the machine to 4x the CPU and RAM ("vertical scaling") and announces the capacity problem is solved permanently. Given the metrics below, predict what happens to (a) throughput headroom and (b) the system's exposure to outages, and say whether "solved permanently" is a fair characterization.
exercises.code:
BEFORE resize:
  1 server, 8 vCPU, CPU util 92% at 500 req/s
  Uptime SLA target: 99.95%

AFTER resize:
  1 server, 32 vCPU, CPU util ~23% at 500 req/s (projected)
  Number of servers: still 1
hints: Throughput headroom and availability risk are two different axes -- work out what changed and what didn't change between BEFORE and AFTER.
Count how many independently-failing machines exist in each scenario. Did that number change?
"Solved permanently" would require the ceiling to never be hit again AND the failure mode to have improved -- check both halves separately.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Throughput headroom improves a lot (CPU util drops from 92% to ~23%, so the service can now absorb roughly 4x the traffic before hitting the same CPU pressure). But outage exposure is unchanged: there is still exactly one server, so any hardware fault, kernel panic, forced reboot for patching, or cloud host-level incident takes the checkout service down just as before. "Solved permanently" is not fair: capacity is solved until traffic grows about 4x again (and at some point no bigger box exists, or its price is absurd), and availability, which never depended on machine size, is not solved at all.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Vertical scaling moves the capacity ceiling further away for the same single machine. It has no effect on the number of independent fault domains, which stays at one. The drop from 92% to ~23% CPU is useful headroom, but "permanent fix" mixes two problems: capacity (fixed for now, will recur) and availability (untouched, because resizing never produces a second machine to fail over to). To judge a 99.95% SLA, about 4.4 hours of downtime a year, ask what happens when this one machine fails. The answer is the same as before: a total outage. The 4x of headroom will also run out one day, and the next resize costs more than this one.

exercises.prompt: A team's capacity plan claims: "We scaled our app tier from 2 to 40 servers behind a load balancer, so we can now handle 20x the traffic." Under load testing, throughput plateaus at about 3x, not 20x. Find the architectural assumption that's wrong.
exercises.code:
ARCHITECTURE:
  [Load Balancer] -> 40x app servers (stateless, each identical)
                          |
                          v
                  1x PostgreSQL instance (single, un-replicated, un-sharded)
                  -- every app server reads AND writes to this same instance
                  -- no read replicas, no caching layer, no sharding
hints: 40 app servers were added, but look at what's directly downstream of all of them -- did that layer get scaled too?
Throughput plateauing well below the theoretical N-times number is the classic signature of a single shared bottleneck that didn't scale with everything in front of it.
Ask: if you added 400 app servers instead of 40, would the plateau move at all?
exercises.solutionCode:
FIXED ARCHITECTURE (one of several valid directions):
  [Load Balancer] -> 40x app servers (stateless)
                          |
              +-----------+-----------+
              v                       v
      1x Postgres primary      4x Postgres read replicas
      (writes only)            (reads, load-balanced across replicas)
                    + a caching layer (e.g. Redis) in front of the DB
                      for hot read paths
exercises.solutionExplanation: The team scaled the stateless app tier 20x but left the one stateful resource every request depends on, the single Postgres instance, unscaled. Once enough of the 40 app servers are busy enough to saturate that one database's connection, CPU, or IO capacity, adding a 41st, 100th, or 400th app server buys nothing, because the bottleneck was never the app tier's capacity to accept requests, it was the database's capacity to serve them. This is a very common horizontal-scaling mistake: scaling the easy stateless layer while ignoring the stateful one that gates end-to-end throughput. Forty servers each holding a connection pool of 20 also means 800 Postgres connections, which can make things worse by itself, since each Postgres connection is a separate server process using memory and scheduler time. The quick check for this class of problem is to ask which component every request passes through and how many copies of it exist. The fix has to address the database: read replicas for read-heavy load, a cache in front of hot reads, or sharding for write-heavy load.

assessments.prompt: A team scales its web tier from 4 to 40 servers behind a load balancer, but observes that peak-load latency barely improves. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The load balancer is misconfigured and cannot handle more than 4 backend servers.
Horizontal scaling has a fundamental hard limit of about 4-10x, regardless of workload.
Some shared downstream resource (a database, a cache, a lock, a third-party API) is saturated.
Adding more servers to a load balancer always increases network latency proportionally, canceling out the extra capacity.
assessments.explanation: The wrong layer was scaled. The app tier can accept far more concurrent requests, but if they all wait on one saturated resource downstream, extra app servers only lengthen the queue in front of it. The “The load balancer is misconfigured and cannot…” option is wrong: load balancers routinely handle far more than 40 backends. The “Horizontal scaling has a fundamental hard limit…” option is wrong because there is no universal limit; it depends on where the bottleneck sits. The “Adding more servers to a load balancer…” option is wrong: a load balancer adds a small, roughly constant latency per hop that doesn't grow with backend count.

assessments.prompt: A stakeholder asks: "Why can't we just buy the biggest possible database server and call our availability problem solved?" Explain, in terms a non-distributed-systems engineer could follow, why a single machine -- no matter how large -- cannot satisfy a high-availability requirement on its own, and what actually has to change architecturally.
assessments.modelAnswer: Machine size and machine count answer two different questions. Size determines how much traffic or data one machine can handle before it runs out of CPU, memory, or IO, and buying a bigger machine does raise that ceiling. Availability is about what happens when something breaks: a disk failure, a kernel panic, a botched OS patch, the host losing power, or a routine maintenance reboot. A single machine of any size is always one such failure away from being down. Buying a bigger single machine does not create a second, independent thing that could take over when the first one is down; it makes the one existing thing faster and leaves the number of independent fault domains at one. A 99.99% (or any serious) uptime target is a statement about tolerating failures, so it can only be promised with at least two machines that can fail independently of each other, with a mechanism (replication for data, a load balancer or failover process for traffic) to keep serving requests when one of them is down. Capacity asks "is this box big enough?"; availability asks "what takes over when this box dies?", and spending more on one box never answers the second question.

assessments.prompt: In the cost curve this lesson describes for the largest machines, why does 'vertical scaling hits a ceiling' involve more than just 'eventually there's no bigger box to buy'?
options: Because larger instances are billed hourly while smaller ones are billed per-second, making cost comparisons unfair.
Because price-per-unit-of-capacity (e.g., price per vCPU) typically increases once you need the largest, most specialized machines.
Because vertical scaling always requires extended downtime to migrate to a new machine, and downtime cost dominates the calculation.
Because cloud providers legally cap the amount of compute any single customer can rent, regardless of price.
assessments.explanation: There is a physical ceiling (a largest machine exists) and an economic one that usually arrives first: past the mainstream families, price per vCPU climbs, from 1.00x to 1.75x in the illustrative table. The “Because larger instances are billed hourly while…” option is about billing granularity, which doesn't create a ceiling. The “Because vertical scaling always requires extended downtime…” option overstates it: a resize usually costs a short restart, or a brief failover if there is a standby. The “Because cloud providers legally cap the amount…” option is fabricated. Providers set account quotas, but those can be raised and aren't legal caps.

assessments.prompt: A team says: "We upgraded from 10 to 40 app servers, so we now have exactly 4x the throughput capacity." When is this claim true?
options: Always, as long as the load balancer is configured correctly.
Never -- horizontal scaling capacity gains are always sublinear regardless of workload.
Only if all 40 servers are the exact same instance size as the original 10.

Only if each unit of work is fully independent and never needs to touch shared state such as a common database, cache, or lock -- otherwise some of the added capacity is consumed by contention and coordination overhead rather than useful work.
assessments.explanation: "N times the servers gives N times the capacity" only holds for embarrassingly parallel workloads with no shared state. The moment servers share a database, cache, or lock, some capacity is consumed by contention instead of useful work. In the extreme, if a shared bottleneck is already saturated, adding more servers in front of it buys no additional throughput at all. The “Always, as long as the load balancer…” option ignores this: no load balancer setting removes a shared bottleneck. The “Only if all 40 servers…” option misses the problem: identical servers still contend for the same shared state. The “Never -- horizontal scaling capacity gains…” option overstates the point: independent workloads can scale linearly.

assessments.prompt: Per the "Choosing Between Them: Sequencing, Not Ideology" section, which of the following is a valid, independent reason to move from vertical to horizontal scaling, distinct from simply having hit a capacity ceiling?
options: An availability requirement (e.g., a 99.99% uptime SLA) that no single machine can satisfy on its own, because one machine -- however large -- is always exactly one fault domain.
The application was originally written in a language that doesn't support multithreading, so adding more cores to the same machine would leave most of the new hardware sitting idle.
The current cloud provider's largest instance type became slightly cheaper this quarter.
The engineering team finds distributed systems more technically interesting to work on.
assessments.explanation: Two separate forces justify moving to horizontal scaling: hitting the vertical ceiling (capacity or cost), or an availability requirement that no single machine can meet, since one machine is one fault domain. The “The engineering team finds distributed systems more…” option is a preference, not an architectural justification. The “The current cloud provider's largest instance type…” option would, if anything, reduce pressure to move off vertical scaling. The “The application was originally written…” option describes a language limitation, which is another reason vertical scaling may not add capacity, and has nothing to do with availability.

concepts.title: Load Balancing and Statelessness
concepts.description: Horizontal scaling only works if requests can be spread across machines safely. That requires a load balancer to decide where each request goes, and stateless services so it doesn't matter which machine actually handles it.
learningObjectives: Explain the role of a load balancer and compare round-robin, least-connections, and consistent-hashing strategies.
Explain how health checks let a load balancer route around failed instances.
Define statelessness precisely and explain why it's a prerequisite for effective horizontal scaling.
Identify hidden sources of state (in-memory session data, sticky sessions, local file writes) that silently break horizontal scaling.
Explain the tradeoff sticky sessions introduce and when externalizing state is the better fix.

sections.heading: What a Load Balancer Does
sections.body:
A load balancer sits in front of a pool of backend servers and decides which one handles each incoming request or connection. Without it, clients would need to know about every backend and distribute the load themselves.

Load balancers generally operate at one of two levels. **L4 (transport-level)** balancers work with IP addresses and ports: they route TCP or UDP connections without looking inside the traffic, which is fast but blind to the request's content. **L7 (application-level)** balancers understand the protocol running on top. For HTTP, they can route on the URL path, headers, or cookies, for example sending `/api/*` to one pool of servers and `/static/*` to another. A load balancer's other job is **health checking**, covered below: deciding which backends are fit to receive traffic right now.

sections.heading: Load Balancing Strategies: Round Robin, Least Connections, Consistent Hashing
sections.body:
**Round robin** rotates through backends in a fixed order: request 1 to server A, request 2 to server B, request 3 to server C, request 4 back to server A, and so on. It gives every backend the same number of requests, but it has no idea how expensive a request is or how busy a backend still is with earlier ones.

**Least connections** routes each new request to whichever backend currently has the fewest active connections (or in-flight requests). Unlike round robin, this adapts to how busy each backend really is: if one backend is stuck on a slow request, its count stays high and new requests go to backends that are actually free. Watch one edge case: a backend that fails fast (returning errors in 1 ms) always has the fewest connections, so without a health check it attracts most of the traffic.

**Consistent hashing** routes based on a hash of some key in the request (a client ID, a cache key, a user ID) so that the same key tends to land on the same backend every time, which lets that backend build a useful local cache for its keys. That matters for any caching layer or sharded backend sitting behind the load balancer. The "consistent" part matters when the pool changes size. With `hash(key) % N`, going from 4 servers to 5 moves about 80% of keys, so nearly every cache goes cold at once. Consistent hashing moves only about 1/5 of them.

sections.heading: Health Checks: Knowing Which Backends Are Alive
sections.body:
A load balancer that routes to a dead backend sends users to failure. To avoid that it checks each backend continuously, typically by hitting a dedicated health endpoint (or passively watching for failed requests) and removing any backend that fails enough consecutive checks from rotation. A typical setup probes every few seconds and pulls a backend after two or three failures in a row.

The eight-server pool from the previous lesson only degrades gracefully *if* the load balancer notices the dead one. Three details decide whether it does. A health endpoint that returns "200 OK" without touching anything a request needs can report healthy while the request path is broken. The opposite mistake is as dangerous: if every instance's check fails whenever the shared database is slow, the load balancer removes all of them at once and a slowdown becomes a full outage, so many teams check only what is local to the instance. Recovery has its own failure mode. When a batch of backends comes back at once (after a deploy, or when a shared dependency returns), they are all marked healthy together and receive a flood of traffic, a thundering herd that can knock them over again. A "slow start" setting ramps a returning backend's share up gradually instead.

sections.heading: Statelessness: The Precondition for All of This to Work
sections.body:
A **stateless** service handles a request using the request itself plus whatever it can fetch from a shared external store. It relies on nothing its own process remembers from an earlier request. That makes the backends interchangeable: the load balancer can route however it wants, and instances can be added, removed, or replaced without anyone noticing.

A **stateful** service keeps something important (session data, an uploaded temp file, the user's cart) in one process's memory or on its local disk, so that instance becomes special. The usual quick fix is **sticky sessions**, configuring the load balancer to always route a given client's requests to the same backend. That brings the single point of failure back for each user: if their backend goes down, their session goes with it, however many healthy backends remain. Every autoscaling scale-in and every rolling deploy now logs people out. With stateless instances, both are routine. Look for hidden state before you scale out: an upload written to local disk and processed by a later request, a rate-limit counter in a module-level variable, a WebSocket registry held in memory, a scheduled job that assumes it runs on only one machine. Each works with one server and breaks with two, often only for some requests, which is why the bugs look random.

sections.heading: Externalizing State: Making "Stateless" Practical
sections.body:
Applications still have state: who's logged in, what's in their cart, what they last searched for. Being stateless means that data isn't pinned to one process's memory. Two patterns are common.

The first pushes state into the client: a signed token (most commonly a JWT) carries the relevant data and is sent back to the server on every request. The server verifies the signature and reads what it needs from the token, remembering nothing locally. This saves a network round-trip, but tokens travel on every request, so they must stay small, and revoking one before it expires (e.g., logging a user out early, or responding to a compromised account) is awkward, since the server issuing the token isn't the one holding it.

The second pushes state into a shared external store -- a database, or more commonly a fast cache like Redis -- that every instance can reach identically. This keeps individual requests simple and keeps revocation trivial (delete the record), but it adds a network hop to every request that needs the state, and the store itself has to be available and fast enough not to become the new bottleneck. Many systems combine the two: a short-lived JWT (minutes) plus a revocable refresh token kept in the store. Neither pattern removes state. Both move it somewhere every instance can reach on equal terms.

examples.title: Round Robin vs. Least Connections Under Uneven Request Cost
examples.code:
Backends: A, B, C
Load balancer policy: round robin (strict rotation A -> B -> C -> A -> ...)

Request sequence and costs: 80ms, 80ms, 8000ms ("generate report"), 80ms, 80ms, 80ms, ...

Round robin assigns:
  req1 (80ms)   -> A
  req2 (80ms)   -> B
  req3 (8000ms) -> C   <- C is now busy for the next 8 seconds
  req4 (80ms)   -> A
  req5 (80ms)   -> B
  req6 (80ms)   -> C   <- queues BEHIND the still-running 8s report on C!
examples.explanation: Assume each backend processes one request at a time. Round robin decides by rotation position and ignores how busy a backend is. Once C draws the 8-second report request, round robin still dutifully sends C its next scheduled request (req6) three turns later, and that cheap 80ms request waits up to 8 seconds behind the report. Least-connections behaves differently: it tracks in-flight work per backend, so while C is busy, new requests go to A or B. Servers that handle many requests concurrently soften the effect but don't remove it, because the report still consumes C's CPU and memory. Equal request counts are not equal load once request costs vary, and least-connections is built to close that gap.

examples.title: Sticky Sessions Reintroducing a Single Point of Failure
examples.code:
Load balancer, sticky sessions enabled (routes by session cookie):

  User X's browser -> [LB] -> always routed to Backend 2 (pinned via cookie)

  Backend 1: healthy, idle
  Backend 2: CRASHES -- holds User X's entire in-memory session/cart
  Backend 3: healthy, idle

  Result: User X's session and cart are gone, even though 2 of 3 backends
  are perfectly healthy and could have served the request just fine.
examples.explanation: Sticky sessions solve the routing half of the state problem (same user, same backend) and leave the fragility. User X's data never left Backend 2's memory, so it dies with Backend 2, and the two healthy backends can't help because they never had a copy. If the cart lived in Redis, whichever backend takes over after Backend 2 is marked unhealthy could serve it without interruption. That is the failure that motivates moving state out of the instances entirely.

examples.title: Externalizing Session State with Redis
examples.code:
# Fragment: needs the redis-py package and a reachable Redis server
import json
import time
import uuid

import redis

# BEFORE: state lives in one process's memory -- breaks horizontal scaling
sessions = {}  # in-process dict, unique to THIS server instance

def handle_login(user_id):
    session_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    sessions[session_id] = {"user_id": user_id, "logged_in_at": time.time()}
    return session_id

def handle_request(session_id):
    session = sessions.get(session_id)  # only found if THIS instance handled login
    ...

# AFTER: state lives in a shared external store -- any instance can serve any request
r = redis.Redis(host="cache.internal", port=6379, decode_responses=True)

def handle_login(user_id):
    session_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    data = {"user_id": user_id, "logged_in_at": time.time()}
    r.set(f"session:{session_id}", json.dumps(data), ex=3600)  # expires in 1 hour
    return session_id

def handle_request(session_id):
    raw = r.get(f"session:{session_id}")  # reachable from ANY instance
    session = json.loads(raw) if raw else None
    ...
examples.explanation: The BEFORE version breaks the moment the load balancer sends a follow-up request to a different instance than the one that handled login: that instance's own `sessions` dict never saw this `session_id`, so the user appears logged out right after logging in. The AFTER version moves the data into Redis, so it no longer matters which instance serves a request. Two details: a Redis value is a string or bytes, so the dict is serialized with `json.dumps` (passing a dict to `r.set` raises `DataError`), and `ex=3600` makes abandoned sessions expire by themselves. The state hasn't disappeared, it has moved. The cost is that Redis must now be available and fast, but Redis is built to be shared and replicated, and a web server's process memory is not.

misconceptions.description: Round robin load balancing is "fair," so it's always the right default choice.
misconceptions.clarification: Round robin is fair in the narrow sense of "equal number of requests per backend," but that's not the same as "equal load per backend" when individual requests vary in cost: a fast query, a slow report, a backend pausing for garbage collection. Least-connections accounts for in-flight work and is usually the better default when request costs vary, because round robin's equal counts can still pile new work onto the backend that is already stuck.

misconceptions.description: Sticky sessions are a perfectly fine way to add statefulness back once you already have a load balancer, since the load balancer "remembers" where to send each user.
misconceptions.clarification: Sticky sessions solve the routing problem (same user, same backend) but leave the fragility: that user's session depends on one backend staying up, which recreates a single point of failure at the scale of one user's experience. They also undermine load balancing, since traffic can no longer be redistributed evenly if one sticky-pinned backend happens to accumulate a disproportionate share of "heavy" users. Externalizing the state (a shared store, or a signed token) removes the need for stickiness and is the more robust fix.

exercises.prompt: A load balancer uses simple round robin across 3 backend instances. One request type ("generate report") takes 8 seconds; all other request types take about 80ms. Traffic is a mix of 1 report request per 10 requests, arriving steadily. Predict what happens to overall latency over time, and explain why round robin doesn't self-correct for it.
exercises.code:
Backends: A, B, C
Load balancer policy: round robin (strict rotation A -> B -> C -> A -> ...)
Traffic pattern: request costs = [80ms x9, 8000ms x1], repeating in that pattern
hints: Round robin decides where to send the NEXT request based only on rotation order -- does it look at how busy a backend currently is?
Trace which backend gets the 8-second report request in each cycle of 10, and think about what else gets routed to that same backend shortly after, before the report finishes.
If a backend is still processing an 8-second request when round robin sends it 3 more 80ms requests, what happens to those 3 requests?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Because round robin routes purely by rotation position and has no idea how busy a backend is, whichever backend lands the 8-second report request keeps getting new 80ms requests assigned to it on schedule anyway. Those requests queue behind the still-running report (assuming each backend works through its requests one at a time). This produces periodic latency spikes: roughly every 10 requests, one backend accumulates a queue of several 80ms requests stuck waiting behind one slow one, so their latency balloons even though they are cheap, and users on those requests see a slow page that has nothing to do with what they asked for. This never self-corrects, because round robin's decisions don't depend on outcomes: it will send another report request (and pile more queued work behind it) on the very next cycle.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Round robin only tracks whose turn is next. When backend B happens to draw the 8-second report request, the load balancer still sends B every third request, and those sit behind the report while A or C may be idle. Least-connections tracks how many requests are in flight per backend, sees B's outstanding one, and sends the next 80ms requests to A or C. Equal request counts are not equal load when one request costs 100 times another.

exercises.prompt: After moving a web app from 1 server to 4 servers behind a load balancer, users report being randomly logged out and sometimes seeing an empty shopping cart mid-session. Here's a simplified version of the relevant code, running identically on all 4 instances. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: carts is a plain Python dict living in one process's memory. When the load balancer sends the next request from the same browser, is it guaranteed to land on the same one of the 4 instances?

Without sticky sessions configured, a typical load balancer (e.g. round robin or least-connections) has no notion of "this user" -- it just balances requests. What does that mean for two consecutive requests from the same session_id?
The fix isn't about making the dict thread-safe -- it's about where the data lives at all.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is that `carts` is an in-memory Python dict, private to each of the 4 processes. The bug only appeared with the second instance. With a single server every request hit the same `carts` dict, so everything worked by accident. Once the load balancer distributes requests across 4 instances (with no stickiness), `add_to_cart` might run on instance 2 while the next `get_cart` for the same session_id runs on instance 4, whose `carts` dict never received that item, hence the empty cart. The same mechanism explains random logouts if session/login state is stored the same way. The fix moves the cart data out of any single process's memory into a shared external store (Redis here) that every instance can read and write, so any of the 4 can handle any request. `decode_responses=True` makes redis-py return `str` instead of `bytes`, so `get_cart` still returns the same kind of items it did before.

assessments.prompt: A team enables sticky sessions on their load balancer to fix a bug where users' shopping carts kept disappearing after scaling to multiple servers. What is the main long-term downside of this fix compared to externalizing session state to a shared store?
options: Sticky sessions pin each user to one specific backend instance.
Sticky sessions only work with round-robin load balancing and cannot be combined with health checks.
Sticky sessions are slower for every single request, even when nothing goes wrong.
Sticky sessions require rewriting the entire application in a different programming language.
assessments.explanation: Sticky sessions fix the immediate symptom (routing) but not the fragility: the user's data still lives on one instance, so that instance is a single point of failure for every user pinned to it, and the load balancer loses some of its freedom to spread load evenly since it must keep sending certain users to certain backends regardless of current load. The “Sticky sessions are slower for every single…” option is wrong: a cookie or header check adds negligible per-request overhead. The “Sticky sessions require rewriting the entire application…” option is absurd: stickiness is a load balancer setting and the application is untouched. The “Sticky sessions only work with round-robin load…” option is wrong: stickiness works with most balancing strategies and with health checks, although a failed check on a pinned backend still strands that backend's sessions.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to a developer who has only ever run a single server, what "statelessness" means for a web service, why it matters specifically for horizontal scaling, and how real applications that clearly do have state (logins, carts, uploads) achieve it in practice.
assessments.modelAnswer: A stateless service still has data: almost every application needs to remember who's logged in, what's in a cart, or what a user uploaded. Stateless means that no single server process is the only holder of that data, so any instance, given the request and the same shared resources, can produce the same correct result. This matters for horizontal scaling because a load balancer, by default, treats all backend instances as interchangeable and does not guarantee that two requests from the same user land on the same instance. If a service keeps meaningful data in one process's local memory (a plain in-memory dict, a variable, a local file), then that user's next request might hit an instance that has never seen it, producing bugs that look random and are maddening to reproduce: logged-out users, vanishing cart items, missing uploads. Applications solve this by moving that state somewhere every instance can reach identically: either an external shared store (a database or a cache like Redis) that all instances query over the network, or by pushing the state into the request itself, most commonly as a signed token (like a JWT) that the client sends back on every request, which the server can verify and read without remembering anything locally. Uploaded files go to shared object storage for the same reason. Either way the state still exists; it is just no longer pinned to the memory of one arbitrary machine that happened to serve an earlier request. The choice between a store and a token comes down to cost per request and revocation: the store adds a network call but a session can be deleted at once, while a token needs no lookup but stays valid until it expires.

assessments.prompt: What is the key functional difference between an L4 (transport-level) and an L7 (application-level) load balancer?
options: L4 balancers only work with UDP, while L7 balancers only work with TCP.

L4 balancers route on IP address and port without inspecting the traffic's content, while L7 balancers understand the application protocol (e.g., HTTP) and can route based on things like URL path, headers, or cookies.
L4 balancers can only be used on-premises, while L7 balancers are cloud-only.
L4 balancers require the backend to be stateless, while L7 balancers work equally well with stateful backends.
assessments.explanation: L4 works with IP addresses and ports and is blind to request content. L7 understands the protocol running on top (e.g., HTTP), which allows content-based routing such as sending /api/* to one pool and /static/* to another. The “L4 balancers only work with UDP, while…” option misstates the distinction: L4 balancers handle both TCP and UDP. The “L4 balancers can only be used on-premises…” option is fabricated; deployment location has nothing to do with OSI layer. The “L4 balancers require the backend…” option is wrong: whether backends hold state is separate from which layer the load balancer inspects.

assessments.prompt: A system uses consistent hashing to route requests to a pool of backend servers that each maintain a local cache. Why is consistent hashing well-suited to this setup, compared to round robin?
options: Consistent hashing guarantees perfectly equal request counts across all backends at all times, which round robin cannot do.
Consistent hashing is simply faster to compute than round robin, so caching workloads pick it for its speed.
Consistent hashing routes the same key to the same backend repeatedly, letting that backend build a useful local cache for that key.
Consistent hashing eliminates the need for health checks because it never routes to an unhealthy backend.
assessments.explanation: Consistent hashing routes on a hash of a key, so the same key keeps reaching the same backend and that backend's cache becomes useful. When the pool changes size, only a small fraction of keys move, where hash-and-mod would reshuffle most of them. The “Consistent hashing guarantees perfectly equal request counts…” option is false: round robin is the one that equalizes request counts, and consistent hashing can distribute unevenly, especially with hot keys. The “Consistent hashing eliminates the need for health…” option is fabricated: a hash says nothing about whether a backend is alive. The “Consistent hashing is simply faster to compute…” option is wrong: hashing a key costs more than advancing a round-robin counter.

assessments.prompt: A backend's health check endpoint simply returns HTTP 200 OK unconditionally, without checking whether it can reach its database. What failure mode does this create?
options: It has no downside, since the load balancer only cares that the process is running at all.
It causes a thundering herd, where all instances receive traffic simultaneously right after a deploy.
It forces the load balancer to fall back to sticky sessions for that backend.

It creates a false-positive health check: the load balancer keeps routing real traffic to an instance that reports healthy but cannot actually serve requests correctly because a real dependency it needs is down.
assessments.explanation: An endpoint that returns "200 OK" without exercising anything the request needs can report healthy while the request path is broken: a false positive. The “It has no downside, since the load…” option ignores that a running process can still fail every request. The “It causes a thundering herd, where all…” option describes a different issue (backends flooded as they recover). The “It forces the load balancer to fall…” option is fabricated; health checks don't turn stickiness on.

concepts.title: The CAP Theorem
concepts.description: Once data is replicated across more than one machine, a network partition forces a choice between staying available and staying consistent. The CAP theorem names that choice and shows why you cannot engineer your way out of it.
learningObjectives: State the CAP theorem precisely: define Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance as the theorem uses them.
Explain why partition tolerance isn't really an optional design choice for a distributed system, which reduces the real-world tradeoff to C vs A.
Walk through a concrete network-partition scenario and determine what a CP system does vs. what an AP system does.
Explain common misreadings of CAP (e.g. "pick any 2 of 3" as a general design menu) and why they're misleading.
Map real systems and technologies to CP or AP tendencies and justify why their designers made that choice.

sections.heading: What C, A, and P Mean
sections.body:
Eric Brewer proposed CAP as a conjecture in 2000; Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch proved a formal version in 2002. It concerns three properties of a distributed data system. **Consistency** means every read receives the most recent write, or an error, as if there were only one copy of the data (formally, *linearizability*). **Availability** means every request to a non-failing node receives a non-error response, though possibly not the most recent value. **Partition tolerance** means the system continues to operate despite messages between nodes being arbitrarily dropped or delayed by the network.

CAP's "Consistency" is not ACID's "C." ACID consistency is about a single transaction never leaving a database in a state that violates its own defined invariants (foreign keys, constraints, application rules): one node's internal correctness. CAP consistency is about agreement *between nodes* holding copies of the same data. A system can be ACID-consistent on every node and still fail CAP consistency, if two nodes disagree with each other about the current value during a partition.

sections.heading: Why Partition Tolerance Isn't Really a Choice
sections.body:
The phrase "pick any 2 of 3" makes CAP sound like a menu: CA, CP, or AP. But designers can't opt out of partitions: cables get cut, switches fail, packets get dropped or delayed, cross-region links go down. Any system with more than one node communicating over a network *will* experience partitions eventually.

So "CA" isn't an option for a multi-node system; it only holds while partitions never happen. The question left is narrower: **when a partition occurs, what does the system do during it?** It can give up consistency (answer anyway, possibly with stale data: AP) or give up availability (refuse some requests to stay correct: CP). While the network is healthy, a well-built system can be both. CAP describes behavior under partition, not a permanent tax. Even then there is a price, which the PACELC extension of CAP names: without a partition you still trade latency against consistency, because waiting for other replicas to confirm takes time.

sections.heading: Walking Through a Partition
sections.body:
Take a value replicated on two nodes, R1 and R2, in two regions. A network partition splits them: they can no longer talk to each other, though clients on each side can still reach their local node. A client on R1's side writes a new value. A client on R2's side then reads, *while the partition is still active*.

A **CP** system's R2 knows it cannot confirm it has the latest value (it can't reach R1 or form a quorum), so it returns an error or times out rather than risk answering incorrectly; the client on R2's side gets no answer, but never gets a *wrong* one. An **AP** system's R2 answers anyway with whatever value it has locally, which may be stale (the write on R1 hasn't propagated yet); the client gets an answer, but it's out of date. CAP permits both; they optimize for different failure costs. Once the partition heals, the AP system needs some reconciliation process to resolve any conflicting writes that happened independently on both sides while split.

sections.heading: Common Misreadings of CAP
sections.body:
Beyond "pick any 2 of 3" (addressed above), two other misreadings come up constantly. First, people treat CAP as the last word on distributed consistency, when most production systems live on a *spectrum*: tunable consistency levels, quorum reads and writes, and bounded staleness windows all let an operator choose, often per operation, how far toward each end of the tradeoff to sit. CAP tells you the tradeoff is unavoidable during a partition; it doesn't tell you how to build a particular system.

Second, people forget that CAP only speaks about behavior *during a partition*. A CP database on a healthy network answers every request, and calling it "unavailable by design" because it is CP is a mistake. Ask how often partitions happen on your network, how long they last, and which requests fail while one is in progress. A single-digit number of minutes a year may be a fair price for never overselling, and an unacceptable one for showing a home page.

sections.heading: Mapping Real Systems to the Tradeoff
sections.body: Systems where an incorrect answer causes serious harm tend to lean CP. Coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd, used for things like leader election and cluster configuration, will refuse to answer if they might be wrong, because two nodes both believing they're the leader ("split brain") does far more damage than a brief unavailability. Systems where users would rather get a fast, possibly-slightly-stale answer than no answer at all tend to lean AP: DNS resolvers serve cached records for a TTL window rather than fail outright; CDN edge caches serve a slightly stale asset rather than fail a page load; NoSQL stores like Cassandra and DynamoDB are commonly run with tunable, often AP-leaning defaults for things like shopping carts and session stores, where brief staleness is a small annoyance and a page that won't load is a lost sale. Each choice is a business judgment about which failure, a wrong answer or no answer, that piece of data can tolerate. It is not a ranking of technologies as better or worse.

examples.title: Reading a Value During a Network Split
examples.code:
Setup: value X = 100, replicated on R1 (US region) and R2 (EU region)

1. Network partition occurs -- R1 and R2 cannot communicate with each other
2. Client in US writes X = 250 to R1  (R1 now has X=250; R2 still thinks X=100)
3. Client in EU reads X from R2, WHILE the partition is still active

CP behavior at R2:
  R2 knows it cannot confirm it has the latest value (no quorum / can't reach R1)
  -> R2 returns an error / times out rather than answer
  -> client in EU gets no answer, but never gets a WRONG one

AP behavior at R2:
  R2 answers with its local value anyway
  -> returns X = 100 (stale -- the US write hasn't been seen yet)
  -> client in EU gets an answer, but it's out of date
examples.explanation: CP treats "return a possibly-wrong answer" as worse than "return no answer," which is right for something like an account balance used to authorize a large withdrawal: you'd rather the system say "try again" than approve a withdrawal against stale data. AP treats "return no answer" as worse, which is right for something like a product page's stock-availability badge, where nobody is hurt by a count that is a few seconds old. Notice that the write in step 2 is also a choice: a strictly CP pair would have R1 refuse it, because R1 can't confirm it with R2 either. With three or more nodes, the side that still holds a majority can keep accepting writes. Once the partition heals, R2 needs to reconcile: pull the latest value from R1, or run whatever conflict-resolution logic the system uses if both sides accepted writes during the split.

examples.title: Mapping CAP Choices to Real Technologies
examples.code:
System / Technology                         Typical lean   Why
ZooKeeper / etcd (config, leader election)   CP             Two leaders elected at once is worse
                                                             than a brief unavailability
RDBMS with synchronous standby replication   CP             Refuses/blocks writes rather than risk
                                                             divergence if the standby can't confirm
Cassandra / DynamoDB (tunable, common use)   AP-leaning     Built for always-on carts and session
                                                             stores; consistency is a per-query knob
DNS                                          AP             Stale records for a TTL window beat
                                                             resolution failing outright
CDN edge caches                              AP             A slightly stale asset beats a failed
                                                             page load
examples.explanation: "Typical lean" is a simplification for the tunable systems. Cassandra sets a consistency level per query, so a `QUORUM` read fails during a partition that a `ONE` read survives. DynamoDB offers eventually consistent (the default) or strongly consistent reads per request, and its writes need a majority of a partition's replicas. Label the operation, then the system. The CP rows are cases where a wrong answer is worse than none (two leaders, a standby that diverges from its primary); in the AP rows users prefer a slightly stale answer now.

examples.title: Why "CA" Systems Don't Really Exist at Scale
examples.code:
Attempt: "we want R2 to be BOTH always available (answers every request)
          AND always consistent (never returns stale data), even during a partition"

During partition (R1 <-x-> R2, cannot communicate):
  Client writes X=250 to R1.
  Client immediately reads X from R2.

  For R2 to be Consistent, it must know about the write to R1 -- but it can't,
  the partition blocks that message.
  For R2 to be Available, it must answer anyway -- but the only value it HAS
  is the old one (X=100), which is not consistent with R1's new write.

  R2 cannot satisfy both simultaneously with the information it actually has.
  It must pick: answer with a stale value (favor A) or refuse to answer (favor C).
examples.explanation: This is CAP's proof by contradiction in miniature. The two guarantees demand opposite actions when a message cannot be delivered, and no code can let R2 return a value it has had no way to learn. The limit is about information, so better engineering doesn't move it.

misconceptions.description: CAP means you get to pick any 2 of the 3 guarantees as a general design choice for your whole system.
misconceptions.clarification: Any system with more than one node on a network will experience partitions (dropped packets, slow links, cut cables) whether it wants to or not, so P isn't something you choose. You choose how the system behaves while one is happening: C or A. Outside a partition, a well-built system can often provide both.

misconceptions.description: CAP's "Consistency" is the same thing as the C in ACID.
misconceptions.clarification: They share a letter and little else. ACID's Consistency is about a transaction never leaving the database in a state that violates its own defined invariants (e.g. foreign key constraints, application-level rules). CAP's Consistency means every client, whichever replica it talks to, sees the same most recent value (linearizability), so it concerns agreement between nodes. A system can satisfy ACID consistency on each node while failing CAP consistency across nodes if those nodes disagree about the current value during a partition.

exercises.prompt: A distributed key-value store is configured as CP. A network partition splits its 5 nodes into a group of 3 (which can still reach each other and form a quorum) and a group of 2 (isolated, no quorum). A client sends a write request to a node in the group of 2. Predict what happens, and why a CP system is designed to behave this way.
exercises.code:
Cluster: 5 nodes, quorum = any 3 nodes that can communicate
Partition: Group A = {node1, node2, node3} (has quorum)
           Group B = {node4, node5} (no quorum, isolated from Group A)
Client -> write request -> node4 (in Group B)
hints: A CP system's defining behavior is that it will sacrifice availability rather than risk an inconsistent write. Does Group B have enough nodes to safely confirm a write?
Quorum requires 3 of 5. Group B only has 2. What should a correctly-behaving CP node do when it can't reach quorum?
Think about what would go wrong if node4 accepted the write anyway, and Group A ALSO accepted a conflicting write to the same key during the same partition.
exercises.expectedAnswer: node4 should reject the write (return an error or time out) rather than accept it, because Group B (2 nodes) cannot form the required quorum of 3. A correctly-implemented CP system refuses to accept writes it cannot safely confirm against enough of the cluster, to prevent a scenario where Group A independently accepts a different, conflicting write to the same key -- which would leave the cluster with two contradictory "confirmed" values once the partition heals, with no principled way to know which one is right. Sacrificing availability for that one write (client gets an error) is the correct behavior for a CP system, not a bug.
exercises.solutionExplanation: node4 sits in the minority partition (Group B, 2 of 5 nodes) and cannot reach enough peers to form a quorum (3 of 5), so it has no way to confirm the write is durable and won't be contradicted by a concurrent write on the other side of the partition. A CP system treats "refuse the request" as the safe outcome: the write fails, and the client must retry (likely once the partition heals, or by finding a node in the quorum-holding Group A). The CP design favors never giving a wrong answer; the AP design favors always giving some answer. An AP system would have node4 accept the write locally and rely on later conflict resolution to reconcile it with whatever Group A did in the meantime.

exercises.prompt: A team builds a distributed cache and advertises it as "always consistent AND always available, even across a network partition, because we wrote very careful synchronization code." Identify the flawed claim, and describe what a correct claim would say instead.
exercises.code:
Design doc excerpt:
  "Our cache replicates data between Node A and Node B. During normal operation,
   writes are synchronously confirmed on both nodes before returning success to
   the client, guaranteeing strong consistency. We also guarantee 100% availability,
   because both nodes independently serve read traffic, so if one node is slow, the
   other answers instead. This holds under all failure conditions, including a
   network partition between Node A and Node B."
hints: What does "synchronously confirmed on both nodes" actually require to be POSSIBLE at the moment of a write?
During an actual partition, can Node A and Node B still synchronously confirm anything with each other at all?
The bug isn't in the synchronization code's correctness -- it's in a claim about what's achievable no matter how good that code is.
exercises.solutionCode:
Corrected claim:
  "During normal operation (no partition), writes are synchronously confirmed on
   both Node A and Node B, guaranteeing strong consistency, and both nodes serve
   reads, giving high availability.

   During a network partition between Node A and Node B, we choose consistency
   over availability: a node that cannot reach its peer to synchronously confirm
   a write will reject that write (or reject reads it cannot guarantee are current)
   rather than risk serving or accepting an inconsistent value. This is a CP system,
   not a CA system -- availability is intentionally sacrificed during a partition
   to preserve correctness."
exercises.solutionExplanation: The flawed claim is "guarantees both, under all failure conditions, including a network partition", the combination CAP proves impossible. If Node A cannot reach Node B, it cannot synchronously confirm anything with it, however careful the code, because the message cannot be delivered. So during a partition, the system has to do one of two things: refuse to confirm the write until it can reach Node B again (sacrificing availability, becoming CP for that operation), or confirm the write locally anyway and reconcile later (sacrificing strict consistency, becoming AP for that operation). No implementation can guarantee both "under all failure conditions"; the document has to say which guarantee bends. Writing it down also tells the teams using the cache what to handle: errors in the first case, stale or conflicting values in the second. The excerpt has a smaller hole too: with synchronous confirmation, one slow node slows every write, so "the other answers instead" only covers reads. A design review should catch both before an incident does.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following best describes what the CAP theorem forces a distributed system to choose between?
options: Whether the system can have more than one replica of its data at all.
Whether the system prioritizes returning a response at all (availability) or refusing to respond rather than risk staleness (consistency) during a network partition.
Whether the system uses SQL or NoSQL as its data model.
Whether the system runs on-premises or in the cloud.
assessments.explanation: CAP's tradeoff appears once a network partition separates nodes holding replicated data: a node cut off from its peers must either answer anyway with data it cannot guarantee is current (favoring availability) or refuse to answer until it can confirm correctness (favoring consistency). It cannot do both for the same request. The “Whether the system uses SQL or NoSQL…” option confuses CAP with a data-modeling choice unrelated to the theorem. The “Whether the system runs on-premises or in the cloud” option confuses it with a deployment/infrastructure choice. The “Whether the system can have more…” option is backwards: CAP only applies once you DO have replicas that can be cut off from each other. A single node makes no CAP tradeoff.

assessments.prompt: A colleague says: "CAP theorem is basically obsolete advice now -- modern databases like Cassandra and DynamoDB just give you both consistency and availability." Explain what's right and wrong about this claim.
assessments.modelAnswer: What's right: modern distributed databases have gotten much better at making the CAP tradeoff feel less painful in practice, mainly by making consistency tunable per operation rather than a single fixed setting for the whole system. Cassandra lets you choose a consistency level per read or write (a quorum of replicas versus one), DynamoDB lets you choose strongly or eventually consistent reads, and outside a partition a well-run cluster can serve available and strongly consistent requests almost all of the time. Partitions are relatively rare in a well-connected data center, so most users never see the difference. What's wrong: the tradeoff hasn't disappeared, it has been made configurable. When a node can't reach enough of its peers to confirm a write or read is current, that same database has to make the CAP choice for whatever consistency level you configured: a request demanding strong consistency will now be rejected or delayed rather than risk staleness (behaving CP for that request), while a request configured for a weaker consistency level will still get an immediate, possibly-stale answer (behaving AP for that request). These systems let you choose, per operation, which side of the tradeoff to be on when a partition happens. CAP isn't obsolete; it has become a configuration setting.

assessments.prompt: A node passes its own internal check that no foreign-key constraint or application invariant has been violated by a transaction, but it disagrees with another replica about the current value of a key during a network partition. What does this scenario illustrate?
options: This is impossible -- ACID consistency and CAP consistency are the same guarantee, so one cannot hold without the other.
The node has violated ACID consistency, which automatically means it has also violated CAP consistency.

The node can be perfectly ACID-consistent (its own internal invariants hold) while the system as a whole fails CAP consistency, because CAP consistency is about agreement between multiple nodes, not a single node's internal correctness.
The node's disagreement proves the system is not partition tolerant.
assessments.explanation: CAP's "Consistency" is not ACID's "C": every node can be ACID-consistent while the system fails CAP consistency because nodes disagree during a partition. The “The node has violated ACID consistency…” option conflates the two guarantees; no invariant was broken on the node. The “This is impossible -- ACID consistency…” option treats two different guarantees as one. The “The node's disagreement proves the system…” option confuses partition tolerance (continuing to operate despite the network dropping messages) with the consistency guarantee at issue here.

assessments.prompt: Coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd are typically built to lean CP rather than AP. Why?
options: Because two nodes simultaneously believing they are the leader ("split brain") is a far more damaging outcome than briefly refusing to answer a request, so these systems favor correctness over responsiveness.

Because leader-election and configuration data changes so rarely that availability doesn't matter for them, and an outage in either of them would go unnoticed by every service that depends on it for several hours.
Because CP systems are always faster than AP systems under normal operation.
Because ZooKeeper and etcd are older technologies that predate AP-style design.
assessments.explanation: Coordination services lean CP because a wrong answer (two leaders at once) does far more damage than temporary unavailability. The “Because leader-election and configuration data changes…” option is wrong: an unavailable etcd is noticed quickly, since a Kubernetes control plane, for example, can't accept changes without it. Its designers accept that cost to avoid split brain. The “Because ZooKeeper and etcd are older technologies…” option is an appeal to age; etcd is younger than Cassandra, which is an AP-leaning store. The “Because CP systems are always faster…” option is false: waiting for a quorum usually makes CP writes slower, and CP vs. AP is about behavior during partitions anyway.

assessments.prompt: A system serves requests that are both fully consistent and always available during normal operation. A partition then occurs, and for its duration the system starts rejecting some requests rather than risk stale answers. Does this contradict the system being "CP"?
options: No, but only because the system must secretly be AP during normal operation and only switches to CP during partitions, which is a design flaw.
Yes -- if the system was ever available and consistent at the same time, it was never really CP in the first place.
Yes -- a true CP system must sacrifice availability at all times, not just during partitions.

No -- CAP is specifically a statement about tradeoffs during an actual partition; outside of a partition, a well-designed system can serve both consistent and available responses simultaneously, and this doesn't make it any less "CP" in how it behaves once a partition actually occurs.
assessments.explanation: CAP does not say a system is always sacrificing one property. On a healthy network it can serve both, and the theorem forces the choice only during a partition. The “Yes -- a true CP system must…” and “Yes -- if the system was ever…” options both wrongly assume CP requires constant sacrifice rather than partition-specific behavior. The “No, but only because the system must…” option calls a flaw what is correct CP behavior: both properties in normal operation, then C over A during a partition.
